questions.q: Why does this lesson say a single, isolated Contact record is the wrong starting point for designing Meridian's onboarding, even for a client who thinks of themselves as an individual?
options: Because FSC does not support individual Contact records at all
Because a single Contact record cannot hold a risk-tolerance questionnaire
Because Account-Contact Relationships are mandatory for compliance reasons unrelated to data entry
Because most clients eventually involve related people or entities (a spouse, a trust), and the household model avoids re-entering the same information separately for each later related account
questions.explain: Clients rarely arrive as truly isolated individuals — a spouse, dependents, or a controlled trust often need to be linked. Designing around the household model from the start avoids duplicate data entry across every later related account, rather than only the first one opened.

questions.q: What is the key architectural difference this lesson draws between a spreadsheet checklist and an Action Plan for onboarding?
options: An Action Plan can track and gate dependent steps based on actual completion status, where a spreadsheet only documents that a process should happen
A spreadsheet checklist is always more accurate than an Action Plan
Action Plans eliminate the need for a compliance review step entirely
There is no real difference; both are equally enforceable
questions.explain: A spreadsheet is documentation of an intended process that depends on someone remembering to follow it. An Action Plan is a system that can block or flag a dependent step (like compliance review) until a prior required step is actually marked complete — directly targeting Meridian's compliance exposure.

questions.q: Why does this lesson insist that Document Checklist Items, not just a task-completion checkbox, matter for Meridian's design?
options: Because Document Checklist Items replace the need for an advisory agreement entirely
Because a checked task box alone doesn't prove the actual signed document exists anywhere retrievable, which is exactly the gap behind compliance's flagged cases
Because tasks and documents are the same object in Financial Services Cloud
Because compliance only cares about task completion timestamps, not documents
questions.explain: Someone could mark 'agreement signed' done without the real signed document existing anywhere auditable. Tracking the document itself as a first-class checklist item, tied to the review step, is what actually closes the specific compliance gap Meridian is trying to fix.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend more than one Action Plan Template rather than one maximally complex template for every client?
options: Because FSC only allows one Action Plan Template per org
Because Action Plan Templates expire after a single use

Because forcing a simple individual client through steps meant for a complex household (like an unrelated compliance review) recreates the "process nobody follows closely" problem, just with more steps
Because templates cannot include a compliance review step
questions.explain: Applying a single complex template to every client regardless of fit adds clutter and irrelevant steps for simpler cases, which undermines the same discipline the redesign is trying to create — multiple templates scoped to actual client structure keep the process relevant to what's really needed.

questions.q: What is the Actionable Relationship Center (ARC) used for in FSC's household model?
options: Tracking metered usage for billing
Generating compliance reports automatically
Replacing the Action Plan Template entirely
Navigating a household's linked relationships (Account-Contact, Account-Account, Contact-Contact) in one view
questions.explain: The ARC is specifically the view for navigating a household's web of linked relationships — spouses, dependents, trusts, and related businesses — rather than a billing, reporting, or task-tracking tool.
